name: astrometry-net
why: Identifies where a photo points in the sky by matching star patterns, real astronomy you can run at home.

brief.what_it_is: Astrometry.net is an open-source program that takes an astronomical image with unknown sky coordinates and works out where in the sky it points. You give it a photo of the sky, and it returns astrometric calibration metadata (a standards-compliant WCS solution for the image) plus lists of known catalogue objects that fall inside the field of view. Its main command is solve-field, which is among roughly fifty executables the package installs, including build-astrometry-index for making index files and a range of FITS and table utilities. The project also runs a public web service at nova.astrometry.net.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says that if you have astronomical imaging with celestial coordinates you do not know or do not trust, Astrometry.net is for you. The authors frame the goal as creating correct, standards-compliant astrometric metadata for every useful astronomical image ever taken, so that the world's astronomical information can be organised, annotated and made searchable.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the matching algorithm in detail. It describes a blind calibration: the image is solved without any prior pointing information, using index files that hold star patterns from a catalogue. The primary reference is the 2010 Lang et al. AJ paper, 'Astrometry.net: Blind astrometric calibration of arbitrary astronomical images', which the README cites for academic use. I did not read the paper, so the details are unverified.

commands_seen.context: Runs the solver from the official Docker image on a local image.jpg, mounting the current directory into the container. This is the README's basic example of using Astrometry.net without a local install.
Solves one of the bundled demo images (apod5.jpg) inside the container, writing results to /tmp. The README says the output appears as /tmp/apod5* files.
Same idea, but mounts a downloaded index directory (/data/index/4100) at /usr/local/data so the solver can use index files that are not shipped with the image.

brief.install_notes: The README only shows a Docker route: the image astrometrynet/solver:0.98 ships with some index files and includes the demo images. For other installs, the README points to code snapshots and releases at astrometry.net/downloads, and the docs have a 'Building/installing the Astrometry.net code' page. I did not fetch that page, so I cannot say what the build needs. Solving real images needs index files, which the docs cover under 'Building Index Files for Astrometry.net'. I did not check where to download them. Note that brew was not mentioned in the README at all.
brief.standout: Blind solving: it needs no hint about where the camera is pointing, and it returns standards-compliant WCS metadata, not just a label. The stated aim is to calibrate every useful astronomical image ever taken, including archival ones.
brief.status: Partly verified. The README copyright runs to 2026, the Docker tag is 0.98, and the README has active build badges (Travis, CircleCI). I did not check the last release date or last commit, so I cannot give a firm date. The README also says 'We are NOT accepting LLM-generated PRs at this time.' Overall it looks maintained, but that is an inference.
brief.caveats: Licensing: the README says parts are 3-clause BSD, but because it links GPL libraries, the whole work must be distributed under GPL v3 or later. Index files are needed before anything solves. The README gives no platform list and does not describe the build. It does not accept LLM-generated pull requests. The docs install page and API pages were not read, so build pain is unknown.
quotes: Input an image and we'll give you back astrometric calibration meta-data, plus lists of known objects falling inside the field of view.

We have built this astrometric calibration service to create correct, standards-compliant, astrometric meta-data for every useful astronomical image ever taken, past and future, in any state of archival disarray.
NOTE: We are NOT accepting LLM-generated PRs at this time.
